newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. envoy Ross holds more talks with Netanyahu.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy Ross holds more talks with Netanyahu.

text.p: U.S. envoy Dennis Ross met Israel's leader Benjamin Netanyahu to press his bid to restore Israeli-Palestinian security ties on Tuesday while Palestinians took to the streets to warn them to lay off Yasser Arafat.
The meeting was their third since Ross arrived in the region at the weekend to try to break a deadlock in peacemaking tightened by a Moslem militant suicide bombing in Jerusalem.
Ross, who has put the focus of his mission on security, made no comment to reporters on his way in to the talks.

He signalled late on Monday, however, that he believed Israel's right-wing prime minister should give some ground on stiff sanctions he slapped on Palestinian areas after the July 30 attack, which killed 16 people including the two bombers.

"Some measures that don't relate so clearly to security are measures that are not helpful and would be counter-productive," he said after meeting Arafat, the Palestinian president, in the West Bank town of Ramallah. He did not elaborate.
In Nablus in the West Bank, witnesses said 10,000 Palestinians took to the streets in protest at U.S. and Israeli pressure on Arafat to clamp down on Moslem militants.
Masked youths in the demonstration burned an effigy of Ross holding a doll resembling Netanyahu.
"This is a message to Ross. Stop U.S. bias towards Israel and stop pressuring the Palestinian Authority to make concessions to Israel," one protester said.

In a slight easing of Israel's clampdown, vegetable trucks from the Palestinian self-ruled Gaza Strip were allowed into Israel on Tuesday but Israel remained sealed tight to tens of thousands of Palestinian workers from Gaza and the West Bank.
PLO officials said Ross would also hold further talks with Arafat on Tuesday. U.S. and Palestinian officials said he was then expected to fly back to Washington.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, eager to bring the sides into accelerated final peace talks, is expected to make her first visit to the region late this month if she deems that enough progress has been made on security cooperation.

Netanyahu, elected last year on a pledge to keep Israelis safe from the bombers, has accused Arafat of granting Moslem militants a haven on territory under his rule and said there can be no movement on peace talks without a crackdown.
Arafat has insisted he is living up to obligations under interim peace deals and accuses Israel of using the bombing as a pretext to wreck the peace process and weaken his legitimacy.

Within hours of his arrival on Sunday, Ross brought together Arafat and Israeli officials for the first time since the bombing. A second meeting among Israeli, Palestinian and U.S. security officials took place in Ramallah on Monday night.

Netanyahu, echoing comments from Ross that results will be the yardstick of success, has said security meetings are "meaningless" unless Arafat cracks down on Moslem militants from Hamas and other movements opposed to peace with Israel.
"They have to fight terrorism. Period," he said on Monday.
Palestinian officials said Monday night's security meeting had focused on laying down a framework for security coordination but had not tackled what measures the sides should take.

They continued to insist on a linkage between security ties and progress on the political front. "Any achievement on the security level without equal progress on the political track will be insufficient," Arafat's adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah said.
Israeli-Palestinian peace talks had already been in stalemate well before the bombing over a Jewish settlement Israel began building in Arab East Jerusalem in March.
Palestinians want construction halted, an end to Israel's demolition of Palestinian houses and land confiscations and a lifting of Netanyahu's punitive measures.
Netanyahu is due in Jordan on Wednesday for talks with King Hussein on the crisis in the peace process. It will be his first meeting with an Arab head of state since the bombing.
In Damascus, Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara was quoted as saying that Syria was still seeking peace with Israel despite the policies of Netanyahu's government.

"The minister told us that he was optimistic despite all conditions...although he said there were not signs of hope with the presence of Netanyahu's government," opposition parliamentarian Saleh Tarif, one of 44 Israeli Arabs who met Shara in Damascus on Monday, quoted the minister as saying.
Sporadic Syrian-Israeli peace talks have failed to resume since Netanyahu's election in May 1996.
